text:
Cold woke him first, before memory did — a cold so total it seemed less a temperature than a subtraction, as though something essential had been drawn out of him and replaced with glass. He lay on his back in the white, and the sky above was a flat, colorless lid. His teeth ached. Behind his eyes a slow pulse beat, the afterimage of the jump, nausea rolling through him in thin waves.

He pushed himself up on one elbow. The snow had begun to settle into the folds of his coat, into the seams, patient as a thief. He knew the arithmetic of this: skin to shivering, shivering to numbness, numbness to a sleep that did not end. Hours. Perhaps fewer.

He got his knees under him. The wind came across the tundra without hurry, carrying grains of ice that stung his cheek, and he turned from it, scanning. A rise of dark rock to the west, low and broken, and beyond it a shadow that might have been a ravine.

He had spent a lifetime learning to arrive. No one had taught him the first thing about surviving it. He started walking, counting his steps, because counting was something to do.

He crossed the rise at a stumble and from the crest saw it: a dark mound in the white, too regular to be rock. He went down. Snow had drifted against one flank; the matted coat held the animal’s shape like a cast. A woolly mammoth. Its trunk lay curled against the snow, one tusk sheared near the root. The body was whole—no cuts, no spear marks, no trampled ring where hunters had stood. Nothing had fed on it. It had lain down, or been caught, and the cold had kept it.

He stood a long time. The wind worked at his coat. He had aimed for the late Pleistocene—the caves, the fires, the people he had spent his life studying. This was older. Tens of thousands of years older. The jump had missed, or he had, and the error was not one he could walk back from. He had given everything to arrive, and here it was: a dead thing in the snow and no one to meet him.

He crouched. His hands were clumsy, but he worked a shard of rib free and tore a strip of hide from the flank, stiff as board. He wrapped the hide around his wrist and put the bone in his coat. Then he looked at the ravine beyond the rise and started walking.

The ravine narrowed as he followed it down, its walls rising until they pinched to a seam of shadow. There, where the stone had split and one slab leaned against another, he found a shallow overhang — no more than a shelf of rock, but it broke the wind, and that was the whole of his ambition now.

He wedged the rib shard upright at the mouth and packed snow against its base, then dragged more with his hands until his arms shook. The hide-wrapped wrist was useless for feeling; he worked by sight and stubbornness, sealing himself behind a low white wall with a bone in it, like an animal building its own grave. He laughed once, briefly, and the sound frightened him.

Inside, he drew out the device. It lay in his palm like a river stone, small and certain. He pressed the charger and waited, and the cold glass gave nothing — no glow, no hum, no answer. He tried again, and a third time, and then he did the arithmetic he had spent his life refusing to do. Decades. It would need decades to gather itself again, and the years here were not the years he had planned for. He put it away.

Dark came down like a lid. Then the sound: a weight moving over snow, deliberate, circling. It stopped. It sniffed. The mammoth's fat was on his coat, and the thing outside knew it, and it did not leave.
